title: A solver race is read on the convergence panel: how fast, how accurate, and on which landscape
summary: Two panels share one story. The left shows where each solver walked on a contour map; the right shows best-so-far objective against cumulative function evaluations on a log axis. The same five solvers on a smooth valley and on a multimodal field give different winners, which is the whole lesson.

media.alt: Two panels. Left: contour map of the Rosenbrock function, a curved narrow valley, with coloured search paths and many purple dots from a genetic algorithm. Right: best-so-far objective value on a log axis from 1e3 down to 1e-11 against cumulative function evaluations from 0 to about 4,700; four curves fall steeply within a few hundred evaluations, an orange dashed curve falls near 1,500 to 2,300, and a purple curve stays near 0.03.

source.caption: Five solvers racing to the Rosenbrock minimum, same evaluation budget
group: 05_05_race_2d_poster: five solvers on Rosenbrock (a curved narrow valley); a text scoreboard at the foot lists final objective and evaluations (the representative figure; a video, this page uses its poster frame)
06_06_race_rastrigin_poster: the same five solvers on Rastrigin, a regular grid of many local minima around one global minimum at the centre (also a video poster frame)
source.note: The caption says 'same evaluation budget', but the scoreboard shows very different evaluation counts per solver (11 to 4685): each solver stops at its own convergence rule within a cap. See 'As drawn'.

read_the_figure.question: Which solver reaches a given accuracy with the fewest function evaluations, and does that ranking survive a change of landscape?
read_the_figure.axes: Left: x1 and x2, the two decision variables, as a contour map coloured by objective f(x, y) on a log colour scale. Right: x is cumulative function evaluations (a shared cost clock, linear); y is best-so-far objective value on a log scale, so each decade down is ten times closer to the optimum.
look_at: On the right panel, a curve that is nearly vertical at the left edge is a solver that converged in very few evaluations. A curve that ends higher than the others stopped without converging.
Compare end heights, not only steepness: the log axis makes 1e-11 and 1e-18 look close, while both are at machine-precision level.
On the left, dots are every evaluation a population method made, a measure of how widely it sampled. A thin line is the path of a method that moves from point to point.
Read the scoreboard at the bottom: it gives final f and evaluations per solver, which the plot can only suggest.
In the Rastrigin race, check which solvers stay near their start: their curves flatten at a plateau far above zero.
read_the_figure.proves: On this one problem and run, the ranking by evaluations to reach a tolerance. It does not prove a general ordering of solver families: the Rastrigin figure is the counter-example in the same project.
if_wrong: A curve that flattens above machine precision is a stalled or local-minimum solver, not a slow one.
If two implementations of the same method (here, two L-BFGS-B codes) differ greatly, suspect settings, the stopping rule or counting of gradient evaluations.
If the cost clocks were not aligned (for example gradient evaluations not counted), the race is unfair.
must_check: One shared cost axis for all solvers, and a statement of how a gradient evaluation is counted.
The same start point for all solvers, with the start and the optimum marked and labelled in the legend.
Log axis for the objective, so that orders of magnitude are readable.
The number of repeated runs or random seeds. A single run is drawn here, and stochastic solvers (CMA-ES, GA) vary between runs.
The stopping rule, since 'same budget' and 'stopped on convergence' are different protocols.
as_drawn: Values are the scoreboard printed under the figures, transcribed exactly.

Rosenbrock (f is the final best objective; evals the evaluations used): Nelder-Mead 1.106e-18, 240; L-BFGS-B native 5.679e-18, 227; CMA-ES 2.921e-17, 2300; L-BFGS-B SciPy 1.074e-11, 197; genetic algorithm 0.02464, 4685.
Rastrigin: CMA-ES 0, 1592; L-BFGS-B native 1.776e-15, 11; L-BFGS-B SciPy 8.882e-15, 24; genetic algorithm 0.5576, 3525; Nelder-Mead 31.84, 114.
CMA-ES needed about 9.6 times Nelder-Mead's evaluations on Rosenbrock (2300 / 240) to reach a similar tolerance, consistent with the 'roughly tenfold' reading.

On Rastrigin, an objective value of 31.84 for Nelder-Mead is near the objective at the marked start point (about (-4, 4)) read from the map, so it did not leave its starting basin. That L-BFGS-B reaches the global minimum from the same marked start in 11 evaluations is surprising, and the figure does not say that all solvers share that start. The caption itself calls the outcome surprising.

terms.meaning: A standard test problem with a long, curved, narrow valley: easy to find the valley, hard to walk along it. Minimum at (1, 1), where f = 0.
A standard multimodal test problem: a bowl overlaid with cosine ripples that create a regular grid of local minima. The global minimum is at the origin, where f = 0.
A derivative-free method that moves a simplex (a triangle in two dimensions) by reflecting, expanding and shrinking it.
A gradient-based quasi-Newton method with limited memory and bound constraints; it builds a curvature estimate from recent gradients.
An evolution strategy that samples a population from a Gaussian and adapts its mean and covariance, so the sampling cloud elongates along a valley.
A population method with selection, crossover and mutation; it uses no derivative and no model of the landscape.
The running minimum of the objective against the number of evaluations; the standard way to compare optimisers.
The ratio of the largest to the smallest curvature at the minimum. A large value means a long thin valley and slow gradient descent.

remember: Compare solvers on best-so-far against cumulative evaluations, with the same counting rule for everyone.
A log axis turns 'ten times closer' into equal steps: read decades, not distances.
The winner depends on the landscape: gradient methods excel on smooth valleys; population methods are the ones with a chance on rugged fields, though neither is guaranteed.
One run of a stochastic solver is a sample, not a rank.
Two copies of the same algorithm should land on the same curve; if they do not, look at settings and counting.

understand.title: Why the valley is hard
understand.text: In a narrow curved valley the gradient points mostly across the valley, not along it. A method with only the gradient zig-zags across the walls. Quasi-Newton methods and CMA-ES both learn the valley's shape, which is why they follow it quickly.

understand.title: Why Rastrigin flips the story
understand.text: Rastrigin is built so that a local descent from almost any start slides into the nearest ripple. Whether a given run escapes depends on the start and step sizes, so one run is evidence of a tendency, not a law.

steps.title: The Rosenbrock gradient and the minimum
steps.note: Setting the second component to zero gives y = x squared; substituting into the first gives x = 1. So the minimum is on the parabola y = x^2, which is the floor of the curved valley you see on the contour map. Checked by substitution.

steps.title: Curvature at the minimum: a thin valley
steps.note: The Hessian at (1, 1) has one direction a thousand times stiffer than the other. Eigenvalues were checked numerically. A condition number of about 2,500 is what makes plain steepest descent crawl here.

steps.title: Steepest descent converges slowly when the valley is thin
steps.note: For a quadratic model with exact line search, the error shrinks by at most this factor each step. At kappa about 2,500 that factor is 0.9992, so thousands of steps would be needed. Quasi-Newton methods approximate the inverse Hessian and escape this limit.

steps.title: Best-so-far on a log axis
steps.tex: \log_{10} f^{\ast}_k\ \text{falls by one unit per decade of improvement}
steps.note: Reading the right panel: a steady downward line on this axis means a constant factor of improvement per evaluation, which is linear convergence. A vertical drop means the solver converged in very few evaluations.

steps.title: Rastrigin: why local minima are everywhere
steps.tex: \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_i}=2x_i+20\pi\sin(2\pi x_i)=0\ \text{has many roots near integers}
steps.note: The cosine term makes the gradient vanish near every integer coordinate, so each is a trap for a local method that starts nearby. Roots are near, not exactly at, the integers.

worked.title: How much did the population method pay on Rosenbrock?
worked.problem: Using the scoreboard, compare CMA-ES (2300 evaluations) with Nelder-Mead (240) and the genetic algorithm (4685), and decide whether the genetic algorithm result is 'a slower version of the others'.

solution.text: Compare final objective values: the genetic algorithm ends at 0.0246, CMA-ES at about 3e-17.

worked.answer: CMA-ES costs about ten times Nelder-Mead; the genetic algorithm costs about twice CMA-ES and ends fifteen orders of magnitude worse. It did not converge in the run drawn, so it is not simply slower; it stopped much higher. That is a different statement from 'needs more evaluations'.

analyze.q: On Rosenbrock the two L-BFGS-B implementations finish at 5.7e-18 and 1.1e-11. Both are 'converged'. Is that a meaningful difference, and what could explain it?
analyze.hint: Tolerance settings and floating-point noise at those levels.

analyze.q: On Rastrigin, Nelder-Mead stops at 31.84 after 114 evaluations. What does the value say about where it stopped?
analyze.hint: Compare with the map value near the marked start.

analyze.q: The caption says 'same budget', but evaluation counts range from 11 to 4685. What protocol does that suggest, and how would it change the race?
analyze.hint: A cap versus a convergence rule.

evaluate.q: A reader concludes 'gradient methods are best' from the Rosenbrock panel. Does the Rastrigin panel overturn it? State what the two figures together do and do not show.
evaluate.hint: One run per landscape, one start point.

evaluate.q: What is the minimum extra information you need before using this figure to choose a solver for your own problem?
evaluate.hint: Dimension, noise, cost of a gradient, many seeds.

create: Redraw the right panel with a median line and an interquartile band over 20 seeds per stochastic solver, and a vertical tick for each solver's stopping point.
Design a third race on a landscape where the gradient is unavailable or noisy, and say which solver you expect to win and why.

checks.q: What does a vertical line at the left of the convergence panel mean?
checks.hint: Many decades of improvement in very few evaluations.
checks.answer: That the solver converged in a handful of evaluations: the best-so-far objective dropped by many orders of magnitude almost immediately.

checks.q: Nelder-Mead used 240 evaluations and CMA-ES 2300. How many times more did CMA-ES use?
checks.answer: 2300 / 240 is about 9.6, so roughly ten times.

checks.q: A solver's curve stops at f = 31.84 on Rastrigin. What does that suggest?
checks.hint: Compare it with the objective value near the starting point.
checks.answer: That it is stuck in a local minimum near its start; 31.84 is close to the value at the start, so it barely improved.

checks.q: Is one race enough to rank solver families?
checks.answer: No. One run on one landscape from one start is a single sample. Rankings need several starts and seeds, and the two landscapes here already give different orderings.

checks.q: How would you test whether L-BFGS-B's Rastrigin success was luck?
checks.answer: Run it from many random start points across the domain and report the fraction that reach the global minimum, with the same protocol for the other solvers.
